VENV := .venv
PY := $(VENV)/bin/python
PIP := $(VENV)/bin/pip

.PHONY: setup test lint fix run

setup:
	test -d $(VENV) || python3 -m venv $(VENV)
	$(PIP) install --quiet --requirement requirements.txt

test:
	$(PY) -m pytest tests/ -v

lint:
	$(VENV)/bin/ruff format --check src/ tests/ ralph.py
	$(VENV)/bin/ruff check src/ tests/ ralph.py
	$(PY) -m mypy --strict src/ tests/ ralph.py

fix:
	$(VENV)/bin/ruff format src/ tests/ ralph.py
	$(VENV)/bin/ruff check --fix src/ tests/ ralph.py

run:
	@test -f src/main.py || { echo "error: no entry point yet — src/main.py does not exist; create it before using make run" >&2; exit 1; }
	$(PY) -m src.main

So far I've read several rule documents (testing, documentation, journal, process) to understand the project's workflow and constraints. I've also inspected the hardware (GPU, RAM, CPU, disk) and the Python environment (requirements, Makefile, pyproject, installed packages, torch version). The hardware check shows a powerful RTX 5090 with ~12.5 GB memory used out of 32 GB, and torch reports a version with CUDA available, indicating GPU acceleration is ready.

The next logical piece of information is the performance expectations or benchmarks for the model I’m supposed to work on. The repository is called MythosMini, described as “A mini Fable: a small language model that runs without a datacenter.” This suggests the goal is to build a tiny model that is efficient in terms of compute and memory, likely targeting the Tiny-ML community. To align my implementation with community standards and to know what metrics matter, I should look up the Tiny‑ML Leaderboard on Hugging Face, which aggregates efficiency and overall scores for tiny models.

I don't have a local copy of that leaderboard, so I need to fetch it from the web. A simple `curl` request to the Hugging Face space URL will retrieve the HTML. I’ll write the output to a temporary file (`/tmp/lb.html`) and also capture the HTTP status code (`-w "%{http_code}\n"`). After downloading, I want a quick glance at the relevant terms present in the page to confirm I got the right content. Using `grep` to extract the words “efficiency”, “overall”, and “leaderboard” (case‑insensitive), then sorting and counting unique occurrences will give me a brief sense of the page’s content without parsing the entire HTML.

Thus, the appropriate next action is to issue a Bash tool call that runs this curl command followed by the grep pipeline. This will provide the needed insight into the Tiny‑ML benchmark landscape, which will guide any model size, quantization, or hardware‑specific optimizations I need to consider later.
